newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Investors wary of BTP outperformance.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Investors wary of BTP outperformance.

text.p: A recent strong showing by Italian bonds (BTPs) raised hopes of further outperformance, but analysts said on Friday that the risks are still considerable.
Talk that the Bank of Italy was about to cut interest rates led BTPs to outperform Bunds sharply, narrowing the spread to 312 basis points from about 320.

"The prospect of weak budgets in the peripheral economies and in the core economies could increase fears that the single currency won't go ahead," said Sally Wilkinson, European economist at UBS in London.
"That will have a disproportionately large effect on the high yielders," she said.
The BTP/Bund spread has narrowed from about 500 basis points in December to a current level of 312.

Huw Roberts, European bond strategist said the prospect of a rate cut, together with dollar strength could push the spread as low as 300 basis points, but it would start to look expensive at that level.
"You might want to look at (BTP) options instead of cash," he said. "You don't want to get caught offside with a cash position."

Although analysts said there is strong scope for a rate cut by the Italian central bank, they add that a move is unlikely before the presentation of the 1997 budget -- expected by the end of September.

Also a cut in rates could jeopardise the recent strength in BTPs. Dealers reported that the Bank of France was seen earlier in the week selling marks for francs, which supported the lira against the German currency.

"While real interest rates are too high, (Bank of Italy governor Antonio) Fazio wouldn't want to put pressure on the lira by cutting rates until the end of the year," said Juli Collins-Thompson, market economist at Yamaichi International in London.
The Italian discount rate is currently 8.25 percent, while the Lombard is 9.75 percent.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government plans to cut the public sector borrowing requirement by 32.4 trillion lire -- an amount which would be bond-positive.
However, Wilkinson said the market has yet to be convinced of whether this can be achieved, as few details have been released.
Collins-Thompson said a fall in BTPs would have a knock-on effect for other high-yielding bond markets -- notably Spanish bonds or Bonos.
"The problem is that there will be wild swings in the BTP/Bund spread as soon as there is any sign of political trouble that will drag down Bonos as well," she said.
The Bonos/Bund spread was forecast to end the year in the 260 to 270 bp region, from a current level of 243, while the BTP/Bund spread would balloon out to 350, she said.

Analysts said Spanish bonds were being supported by strong domestic investor belief that Spain will meet the Maastricht convergence criteria and be in the first round of European Economic and Monetary Union.
But international investors are likely to remain shy of the market until after the budget.
"Spain has priced in so much good news already and its main support is that the domestics think everything is fine," said Roberts. "Italy has more upside potential, as long as the budget goes well."
